scenario_stem:
Kestrel Construction Ltd is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by Daniel Okafor, building houses and small warehouse units in the town of Marlow. It owns one plot of land near the ring road, large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse. The houses would earn $900,000 in revenue over 18 months, while the warehouse would earn $650,000 over 14 months. The business employs 24 site workers and 3 supervisors.

Daniel has only $120,000 saved for materials. He must choose between the housing project and the warehouse, knowing the land cannot do both. He could hire two bricklayers at $450 each per week or lease a concrete mixer for $1,200 a month. Land prices in Marlow have risen 20% since 2023, and the accountant reminded Daniel that scarcity means every choice has an opportunity cost. Either option carries risk, and delays could raise costs by 15%.

questions.question_text: Define 'land' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Land refers to all natural resources used to produce goods and services, such as the plot near the ring road in Marlow and materials like timber and sand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Land = all natural resources used in producing goods and services, e.g. the building plot, timber, sand or land itself
Reward any example of a natural resource input used to make goods or services (2 marks for a clear definition with reference to nature)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why land is important to Kestrel Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Land is a basic factor of production that provides natural resources for making goods [k]. Kestrel's only plot near the ring road is large enough for either 12 houses or a single distribution warehouse worth $900,000 or $650,000 of revenue [app]. Reason 2: Without suitable land the business cannot produce or sell anything [k]. With no plot to build on, the $900,000 house scheme and the $650,000 warehouse scheme would both be impossible and Kestrel would earn nothing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Land provides natural resources / site / raw materials needed for production
Without land the firm cannot produce or generate sales revenue
application_max_2: Reference to the single plot being large enough for 12 houses or the warehouse
Reference to the $900,000 (houses) and $650,000 (warehouse) revenue figures / the Marlow site

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which opportunity cost affects Kestrel Construction Ltd's decision.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made [k]. By choosing the 12 houses, Kestrel gives up the chance to earn $650,000 from the warehouse, so the true cost of the houses includes the lost warehouse revenue [app]. This means Daniel must compare both revenue streams carefully before spending the $120,000 of scarce materials money [an]. Point 2: Scarcity of the single plot means the land cannot serve both projects [k]. Committing the plot to the housing scheme removes the chance to use it for the warehouse, so every scarce input carries a sacrifice [app]. This forces Daniel to recognise that scarcity creates opportunity cost in all of his decisions, not only in this one [an].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone when a decision is made
Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants, forcing economic choices
application_max_2: Reference to forgoing the $650,000 warehouse revenue if the 12 houses are chosen (or vice versa)
Reference to the single plot / the $120,000 materials finance as scarce resources
analysis_max_2: Analysis of how foregone revenue or profits changes the true cost of each option
Analysis chain linking scarcity -> choice -> sacrifice -> better decision-making

questions.question_text: Do you think Kestrel Construction Ltd should build the 12 houses rather than the warehouse? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the houses: Building 12 houses suits Kestrel's construction skills and could earn $900,000 in revenue [k]. That is $250,000 more than the warehouse's $650,000, even though it takes 18 months rather than 14 [app]. However, the scheme ties up $120,000 of scarce materials money and any delay could raise costs by 15%, squeezing the margin for error on a fixed plot [an]. Argument for the warehouse: The warehouse earns $650,000 within 14 months, releasing cash faster for future projects [k]. Land prices have risen 20% since 2023, so completing quickly protects the value of the Marlow plot [app]. But $650,000 is $250,000 less revenue and would leave Kestrel dependent on a single buyer in a weaker warehouse market [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the housing project offers the higher revenue of $900,000 and matches Kestrel's house-building specialism, so it should proceed only if Daniel secures firm buyer contracts and a contingency for the 15% cost risk [eval]. Otherwise the quicker, lower-risk warehouse would be the wiser choice for a business holding just $120,000 in materials finance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Houses give higher total revenue ($900,000 vs $650,000)
Warehouse gives faster cash return (14 vs 18 months) and matches 20% land price rise
application_max_2: Uses $900,000 / $650,000 / $120,000 / 12 houses / 18 months vs 14 months figures from the stem
Reference to the single Marlow plot and the 15% cost-overrun or 20% price-rise risk
analysis_max_2: Analysis of revenue, cash-flow timing and cost-risk trade-offs between the two schemes
Analysis of how the decision affects scarce materials finance and future projects
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that is conditional on contracts/cost risk, or favours the warehouse, supported by stem figures
Balanced judgement recognising the risk of the houses scheme vs the security of the warehouse

scenario_stem:
Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd is a private limited company run since 2019 by sisters Priya and Anita Raman. From a workshop in Fenwick it handcrafts oak dining tables and chairs, employing 14 carpenters paid $38,000 per year and 3 apprentices on $16,000 each. Annual output is 900 tables sold at $520 each. The sisters are considering division of labour so each worker specialises in one stage, such as cutting, sanding, joining or finishing.

At present every carpenter builds a whole table alone. Trials show specialised workers can finish a table in 6 hours instead of 11, lifting potential output to 1,240 tables a year. However, several carpenters fear their jobs will become monotonous and their craft skills will narrow. The workshop would need reorganising into 4 stations, and wages currently cost $580,000 a year. Quality complaints must stay below 3% for the plan to succeed.

questions.question_text: Define 'labour' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Labour refers to the human effort, both physical and mental, used to produce goods and services, such as the 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices working in the Willow & Pine workshop. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Labour = human effort used in producing goods and services
Reward references to physical/mental effort, or workers such as carpenters, apprentices or staff

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why labour is important to Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Labour performs the skilled work needed to create the product [k]. Willow & Pine employs 14 carpenters at $38,000 per year plus 3 apprentices, whose hands craft the 900 tables sold at $520 each [app]. Reason 2: Without labour the business cannot turn timber into furniture [k]. If the carpenters and apprentices stopped work, the $580,000 wage bill would produce nothing and the 900-table output could not be reached [app].

knowledge_max_2: Labour does the physical/mental work of production
Without labour, production is impossible / no goods and services made
application_max_2: Reference to 14 carpenters and 3 apprentices / $38,000 and $16,000 pay
Reference to 900 tables a year at $520 / $580,000 wage bill

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of division of labour for Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Division of labour means workers specialise in one repeated stage of production [k]. Trials show specialised staff can finish a table in 6 hours instead of 11, lifting potential output to 1,240 tables a year [app]. This raises productivity so the $580,000 wage bill is spread over more units and average labour cost per table falls [an]. Point 2: Specialised workers become faster and more skilled at their single stage [k]. Each of the 4 stations such as cutting or finishing would develop deep expertise, keeping quality complaints below the 3% target [app]. This improves customer satisfaction, protects the brand and supports repeat orders from the Fenwick workshop [an].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation in one repeated task / stage of production
Workers become quicker and more expert through repetition
application_max_2: Reference to 6 hours vs 11 hours build time and 1,240 tables a year
Reference to 4 stations and the 3% quality complaint threshold
analysis_max_2: Analysis that higher output per worker lowers average cost / raises profit margin
Analysis that fewer errors improve quality, reputation and repeat sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Willow & Pine Furniture Ltd should introduce division of labour in its workshop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for division of labour: Specialisation would cut build time from 11 hours to 6 hours per table and could lift output to 1,240 tables a year [k]. Average labour cost per table would fall and revenue could rise sharply if demand holds for oak tables at $520 each [app]. However, gains depend on staff accepting repetitive jobs across 4 stations and on quality complaints staying below 3% [an]. Argument against: Whole-table crafting preserves the craft skills that justify premium pricing and keeps workers engaged [k]. Forcing specialisation could trigger boredom and resignations, risking the loss of experienced $38,000-a-year carpenters [app]. This risk is manageable through job rotation and careful deployment of the 3 apprentices, but it cannot be ignored [an]. Overall, division of labour is the better choice because saving 5 hours per table and the chance to reach 1,240 tables a year clearly outweigh the morale risk, provided the Ashbys consult staff and monitor the 3% quality threshold closely [eval]. Otherwise output gains could be cancelled out by turnover, rework and quality claims [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour cuts build time (11 to 6 hours) and can raise output (1,240 tables)
Whole-table crafting preserves skill, variety and worker engagement
application_max_2: Uses 6 hours vs 11 hours, 1,240 tables, 4 stations and $580,000 wage figures from the stem
Reference to monotony fears and the 3% quality complaints target
analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity/cost per unit versus motivation and turnover risks
Analysis of quality outcomes and how they affect revenue and reputation
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation supporting specialisation (or retention) conditional on consultation and quality monitoring
Balanced judgement weighing output gains against craft-skill loss and boredom

scenario_stem:
Crossdock Freight Ltd is a logistics business based in the port city of Dunmore, founded 4 years ago by Marcus Reeve. It runs 9 delivery trucks, employing 21 drivers and 6 dispatchers. Revenue last year was $1,750,000 with a profit of $210,000. The company is winning new contracts carrying food from farms to supermarkets across the region, and truck utilisation is already 92% on a typical day.

To meet demand Marcus must add 3 trucks. Buying them would cost $240,000 plus $38,000 a year in maintenance, and they would last 8 years. Leasing would cost $3,600 per truck per month with servicing included. Marcus has $70,000 available now and could borrow the rest at 8% interest. The new contracts promise an extra $400,000 a year in revenue if the trucks arrive before summer.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Capital refers to man-made resources used to produce goods and services, such as the trucks, forklifts, tools and depot machinery used by Crossdock Freight Ltd. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made resources used in production (goods used to make other goods)
Reward examples such as trucks, machinery, vehicles, tools, equipment or buildings

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why capital equipment is important to Crossdock Freight Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital goods such as trucks are the tools that let the business deliver its service [k]. Crossdock runs 9 delivery trucks carrying supermarket food across the region, and truck utilisation is already 92% on a typical day [app]. Reason 2: Without enough capital equipment the firm cannot accept the new contracts [k]. Winning work worth an extra $400,000 a year is impossible unless 3 more trucks are added to the existing 9 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Capital equipment enables production/delivery of the service
Without adequate capital, output and contract capacity are capped
application_max_2: Reference to 9 delivery trucks and the 92% utilisation rate
Reference to the new food contracts / extra $400,000 a year needing 3 more trucks

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Crossdock Freight Ltd might face if it cannot fund new capital equipment.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Without capital goods the firm lacks the machinery needed to produce more [k]. Without $240,000 to buy 3 trucks, the new contracts cannot be served and the fleet stays overstretched at 92% utilisation [app]. This leads to late deliveries, penalties and damaged relationships with supermarket customers, which could cost the $400,000 revenue opportunity [an]. Point 2: Relying on overworked capital raises running costs [k]. The existing 9 trucks would work beyond capacity, pushing maintenance above the quoted $38,000 a year and increasing breakdown risk [app]. This eats into the $210,000 profit and could leave Crossdock unable to meet food-safety delivery windows [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lack of capital equipment limits production capacity
Overworked/older capital raises maintenance and breakdown costs
application_max_2: Reference to the $240,000 purchase, $38,000 maintenance and 8-year life
Reference to the 92% utilisation and the $400,000 contract opportunity
analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from no new trucks -> lost contracts -> lost revenue and reputation
Analysis chain from overuse -> higher maintenance -> lower profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Crossdock Freight Ltd should buy the 3 trucks rather than lease them? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for buying: Buying for $240,000 plus $38,000 a year maintenance makes the trucks assets lasting 8 years [k]. Owned trucks build equity, lower the true long-run cost per delivery and can be fitted out for the supermarket food contracts [app]. However, with only $70,000 available now, Marcus must borrow $170,000 at 8% interest, adding roughly $13,600 a year to his costs [an]. Argument for leasing: Leasing costs $3,600 per truck per month with servicing included, spreading payments and avoiding big up-front borrowing and maintenance risk [k]. It also gives flexibility to return or upgrade trucks if the new contracts falter [app]. But over a full year, 3 leased trucks cost $129,600 with nothing owned at the end [an]. Overall, buying is the better long-term choice for a stable operator already at 92% utilisation and expecting $400,000 a year in new revenue, provided Marcus secures the loan at 8% and keeps maintenance within $38,000 [eval]. Leasing would suit him only if the contracts were unproven and cash flow were tighter than the current $70,000 suggests [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying = ownership, asset lasting 8 years vs monthly lease of $3,600 per truck
Leasing spreads payments and includes servicing; buying needs borrowing at 8%
application_max_2: Uses $240,000 / $70,000 / $170,000 and $38,000 maintenance figures
Uses $3,600 per month leasing rate and the $400,000 projected new revenue
analysis_max_2: Analysis of 8-year cost comparison: leasing $129,600 a year vs buying plus 8% interest
Analysis of capacity/asset value vs cash-flow flexibility and contract risk
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation favouring purchase (or leasing) conditional on loan/contracts
Balanced judgement weighing ownership benefits vs borrowing risk at 8% interest

scenario_stem:
BrightSpark Printing Ltd is an independent commercial printer in the market town of Wexley, started 8 years ago by owner Rachel Dunne. It employs 12 print operators and 2 sales staff, producing catalogues, labels and posters. Last year revenue was $880,000 and profit $96,000. A national online printer has begun undercutting prices by 25% across the region.

Rachel must decide whether to take the risk of buying a high-speed digital press costing $150,000, doubling capacity and cutting unit costs by 18%, or to keep the current presses and compete on service and 24-hour delivery. The bank will lend $100,000 at 9% interest if needed, with a personal guarantee from Rachel. Failure could endanger the business, but standing still may lose 30% of revenue to the cheaper rival within a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'enterprise' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Enterprise is the risk-bearing and decision-making factor that organises land, labour and capital to produce goods and services, such as Rachel Dunne setting up and running BrightSpark Printing Ltd. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise = the organising / risk-taking factor of production
Reward references to entrepreneurial risk, decision-making or combining the other factors (land, labour, capital)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why enterprise is important to BrightSpark Printing Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Enterprise organises land, labour and capital into a working business [k]. Rachel decides how the 12 print operators, 2 sales staff and machinery combine to produce catalogues and labels earning $880,000 a year [app]. Reason 2: Enterprise drives innovation and response to competition [k]. Facing a national rival undercutting prices by 25%, Rachel must choose how to compete, for example by buying a high-speed press or improving service [app].

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise combines and organises the other factors of production
Enterprise creates change/innovation in response to competition or opportunity
application_max_2: Reference to Rachel organising 12 print operators and 2 sales staff at $880,000 revenue
Reference to the 25% undercutting by the online printer and the decision over the press

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Rachel faces when showing enterprise against the online rival.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Entrepreneurial risk-taking can threaten survival [k]. Buying the $150,000 press with a $100,000 bank loan at 9% interest means failure could leave BrightSpark unable to meet repayments [app]. This would erode the $96,000 profit and could put the 12 print operators out of work [an]. Point 2: Competing on price against a bigger rival squeezes margins [k]. The online firm's 25% price cut may force Rachel to discount up to 30% of revenue to keep clients [app]. This leaves less cash to pay for the new press and weakens long-term investment [an].

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise = risk-taking; risks can threaten business survival
Price competition from a larger rival can erode profit margins
application_max_2: Reference to the $150,000 press and the $100,000 loan at 9% interest
Reference to the 25% undercutting and the possible loss of 30% of revenue
analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from loan repayments -> lower profit -> possible job losses/closure
Analysis chain from discounting -> reduced margins -> less cash for investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Rachel should buy the high-speed digital press rather than keep the current presses and compete on service? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for buying the press: The $150,000 press doubles capacity and cuts unit costs by 18% [k]. That protects margins against the rival's 25% undercutting and lets BrightSpark quote sharper prices while still delivering in 24 hours [app]. However, with $100,000 borrowed at 9% interest and a personal guarantee, repayments would eat into the $96,000 profit and a soft winter could make the upgrade unaffordable [an]. Argument against buying: Keeping the current presses avoids new borrowing and risk, and superior service with 24-hour turnaround could retain loyal clients without the $150,000 outlay [k]. This keeps Rachel flexible while she studies the online rival's real pricing in Wexley [app]. But standing still risks losing up to 30% of revenue within a year as price-sensitive customers switch away [an]. Overall, Rachel should buy the press if her order book shows at least $150,000 of new long-term contracts, because an 18% unit-cost cut is the strongest defence against a 25% price gap and the press would pay back over its 10-year life [eval]. If the pipeline stays soft she should compete on service first and borrow later once demand is proven [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Press costs $150,000, doubles capacity, cuts unit costs 18%
Keeping presses avoids $100,000 borrowing at 9% but risks losing 30% of revenue

analysis_max_2: Analysis of margin protection vs loan-repayment strain and personal guarantee risk
Analysis of capacity gain vs standing still and revenue erosion over a year
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on order pipeline / risk appetite
Balanced judgement weighing cost saving and revenue risk for and against the press

scenario_stem:
Sunvalley Foods Ltd is a food processing company in rural Carlow County, founded 10 years ago by Aoife Brennan. It freezes and packs mixed vegetables for supermarket own-brand ranges, employing 46 production staff plus 4 quality inspectors. Output is 30,000 bags per week across five stages: sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing.

Currently workers rotate through all five stages each week. Aoife wants to introduce permanent specialisation, giving each worker one stage. In similar factories this raised output by 40%, but some Sunvalley staff fear boredom and the firm lost 2 workers after a 3-month trial last year. Training one worker for a single stage costs $800, and rejection rates currently stand at 6% of batches. The board must decide by December whether to change.

questions.question_text: Define 'division of labour'.
questions.model_answer: Division of labour is where production is split into separate tasks and each worker specialises in one task, such as sorting, washing, cutting, blanching or packing mixed vegetables. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour = splitting production into small distinct tasks
Each worker specialises in just one repeated task / stage

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why businesses use division of labour.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Division of labour breaks production into small tasks so workers specialise [k]. Sunvalley splits its line into five stages — sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing — across 46 production staff [app]. Reason 2: It raises productivity and speeds up output [k]. In similar factories specialisation raised output by 40%, which would push Sunvalley well beyond its current 30,000 bags per week [app].

knowledge_max_2: Workers specialise in one repeated task rather than all tasks
Specialisation speeds up work / raises productivity through practice
application_max_2: Reference to the five stages and 46 production staff
Reference to the 40% output gain and 30,000 bags per week from the stem

valid_app_words: sorting, washing, cutting, blanching and packing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sunvalley Foods Ltd might face after introducing specialisation.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Repetitive specialist work causes boredom and lowers motivation [k]. Sunvalley already lost 2 workers after a 3-month specialisation trial last year, showing that single-stage work can demoralise the 46 production staff [app]. This raises recruitment and training costs at $800 per replacement and disrupts the 30,000-bag weekly target [an]. Point 2: Over-dependence on key specialists creates bottlenecks [k]. If the cutting specialist is absent, the whole line can stall because each worker masters only one stage [app]. This risks raising rejection rates above the current 6% and jeopardising supermarket own-brand contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: Monotony/boredom reduces motivation and can raise labour turnover
Over-specialisation creates dependency on individuals, risking bottlenecks
application_max_2: Reference to the 2 workers lost after the 3-month trial and $800 retraining cost
Reference to the 6% rejection rate / possible contract loss
analysis_max_2: Analysis chain from boredom -> resignations -> higher costs and disrupted output
Analysis chain from absence of a specialist -> line stoppage -> missed orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Sunvalley Foods Ltd should introduce permanent specialisation on its production line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for specialisation: Giving each of the 46 production staff one of the five stages could raise output by 40%, easing the strain on the 30,000-bag week [k]. Trained specialists make fewer mistakes, which should help push rejection rates below the present 6% [app]. However, boredom could worsen turnover, following the 2 resignations seen in the 3-month trial [an]. Argument against: Keeping job rotation preserves motivation and flexibility [k], and retraining everyone at $800 each would be wasted if staff keep leaving or demand shifts between stages like blanching and packing [app]. But rotation means slower throughput and caps output at 30,000 bags a week for a growing own-brand range [an]. Overall, permanent specialisation is justified if Aoife combines it with job rotation, structured training at $800 per head and close monitoring of the 6% rejection rate, because the 40% output gain is too large to ignore for supermarket contracts [eval]. Imposing rigid single-task roles without staff consultation would only repeat last year's resignations [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation can raise output by 40% and reduce mistakes
Rotation preserves motivation; rigid tasks risk turnover and training waste
application_max_2: Uses the 40% figure, 30,000 bags, 6% rejections, $800 training cost and the 2 resignations
Reference to the five stages and 3-month trial from the stem
analysis_max_2: Analysis of productivity gains vs turnover/retraining costs
Analysis of quality and flexibility trade-offs for the supermarket range
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on rotation/consultation/monitoring

scenario_stem:
FreshPress Laundry Co is a commercial laundry serving 26 hotels and restaurants across Norwick. Founded 5 years ago by Tomasz Nowak, it employs 18 operatives across two shifts at a single depot. Last year it cleaned 4,200 tonnes of linen, about 233 tonnes per worker, but 45 hotel loads were rejected last quarter for poor stain removal.

Tomasz must choose between buying a high-capacity washer costing $85,000, lifting output to 5,100 tonnes a year but using 15% more electricity, or spending $20,000 on staff training to cut re-washes by 30% and reduce wasted water and detergent. He has $90,000 available now. The hotels have asked for better stain removal by March or they will review contracts worth $140,000 a year. The hotels also expect twice-daily deliveries.

questions.question_text: Define 'productivity'.
questions.model_answer: Productivity measures how much output is produced per unit of input, usually per worker, such as 4,200 tonnes of linen cleaned divided by 18 operatives at FreshPress Laundry Co. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per worker / per unit of input
Reward formula-style definitions or references to output efficiency per labour unit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why productivity is important to FreshPress Laundry Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Productivity shows output per worker, so higher productivity lowers average cost per tonne [k]. FreshPress cleans about 233 tonnes per worker per year, so even modest gains across 18 operatives would cut unit costs sharply [app]. Reason 2: High productivity helps meet customer demand and deadlines [k]. The hotels want stain-removal problems fixed by March or they will review contracts worth $140,000 a year, so more output per worker protects that revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher productivity lowers average/unit costs
Productivity lets the firm meet deadlines and customer demand
application_max_2: Reference to 4,200 tonnes / 233 tonnes per worker / 18 operatives
Reference to the March deadline and the $140,000 hotel contracts

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between productivity and efficiency.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Productivity measures the quantity of output per unit of input, whereas efficiency measures how well inputs are used with minimal waste [k]. FreshPress cleans 233 tonnes per worker, a productivity measure, while 45 rejected hotel loads and poor stain removal are signs of inefficient work [app]. This shows productivity counts volume but efficiency counts quality and waste [an]. Point 2: Productivity gains can come from more machines or longer hours, but efficiency gains come from better methods [k]. The $85,000 washer would raise output to 5,100 tonnes a year even though it uses 15% more electricity [app]. So FreshPress could lift productivity yet waste more resources if efficiency were ignored [an].

knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per input (volume); efficiency = waste minimisation / quality of input use
Productivity can rise with machines or hours; efficiency requires process improvement
application_max_2: Reference to 233 tonnes per worker vs 45 rejected loads
Reference to the $85,000 washer and its 15% extra electricity use
analysis_max_2: Analysis distinguishing volume/quantity measures from waste/quality measures
Analysis that productivity can rise while efficiency falls, with cost consequences

questions.question_text: Do you think Tomasz should buy the high-capacity washer rather than spend $20,000 on staff training? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the washer: The $85,000 washer lifts output to 5,100 tonnes a year, a gain of 900 tonnes [k]. It lets FreshPress take on extra hotel linen and cut turnaround times for its 26 hotels and restaurants [app]. However, it uses 15% more electricity and would absorb nearly all of the $90,000 the business has available, leaving little for maintenance or training [an]. Argument for training: Spending $20,000 on staff training could cut re-washes by 30%, saving water and detergent [k]. It directly addresses the 45 rejected loads that caused the crisis at far lower cost than the washer [app]. But training alone will not raise total capacity or satisfy hotels needing 5,100 tonnes of linen output [an]. Overall, Tomasz should buy the washer because it is the only option that protects the $140,000 contracts, provided he secures an electricity-efficient model, because stain complaints plus lost output together exceed $140,000 a year [eval]. Training should follow in the next quarter to fix quality once the extra capacity is guaranteed [eval].

Training costs $20,000, cuts re-washes 30% but adds no capacity
application_max_2: Uses $85,000 / $90,000 / $20,000 / 5,100 tonnes / 30% figures from the stem
Reference to the 45 rejected loads and $140,000 contracts and March deadline

scenario_stem:
Copperfield Foods Ltd is a family food business in the coastal town of Bowen Bay, producing jams, sauces and pickles. It has traded for 7 years under founder Maria Copperfield, employing 9 staff, with revenue of $640,000 last year. Demand for its tomato chutney has grown 30% since winter, and customers keep asking for sugar-free options, though healthier ingredients cost $0.40 more per jar.

Maria has $30,000 to spend and must choose between buying a new boiling kettle line costing $28,000, or launching a sugar-free jam range costing $26,000 for ingredients and jars. She cannot fund both, so either choice means giving up the other. The new range could add $90,000 in sales if it succeeds. The bank manager reminded her that resources are scarce while customer wants are unlimited.

questions.question_text: Define 'wants'.
questions.model_answer: Wants are things people desire but do not need to survive, such as jams, sauces and pickles, whose demand exceeds the resources available to supply them. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Wants = desired goods/services not essential for survival
Wants are unlimited; resources to satisfy them are scarce

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why scarcity is a problem for Copperfield Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are unlimited [k]. Maria has only $30,000 to spend but wants both a $28,000 kettle line and a $26,000 sugar-free launch [app]. Reason 2: Scarcity forces choices with opportunity costs [k]. Choosing one option means giving up the other, so the scarce $30,000 cannot fund both projects at Copperfield Foods [app].

knowledge_max_2: Scarcity = limited resources vs unlimited wants
Scarcity forces trade-offs / economic choices to be made
application_max_2: Reference to the $30,000 budget vs the $28,000 and $26,000 options

questions.question_text: Explain two ways understanding opportunity cost could help Maria make better decisions.

Weighing the $90,000 potential sales against slower production clarifies the true cost of each option [an]. Point 2: Recognising opportunity cost keeps decisions aligned with customer demand [k]. Tomato chutney demand grew 30% and customers ask for sugar-free jars, so choosing the range matches wants and uses scarce ingredients wisely [app]. This raises the chance the $26,000 investment is recovered, rather than spending $28,000 on capacity for a product customers are not asking about [an].

scenario_stem:
Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd is a woodworking business in the market town of Elmridge, founded 9 years ago by Ben and Clara Ashby. It employs 10 woodworkers making two ranges: hand-carved walnut cabinets at $1,900 each, taking 16 hours to make, and flat-pack pine shelves at $85 each, taking 40 minutes. Annual revenue is $720,000, and the Ashbys want to add value by specialising.

Specialising fully in walnut cabinets would let each worker master one craft, cut waste by 12% and appeal to boutique retailers. However, walnut costs $9 per board foot and demand is uncertain, with only 60 firm cabinet orders for next year. The firm sells 3,000 flat-pack shelves a year and they keep cash flowing. The owners must decide at this month's board meeting which market to serve.

questions.question_text: Do you think Cedar & Co Furniture Ltd should specialise fully in hand-carved walnut cabinets? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for full specialisation: Concentrating on walnut cabinets lets each of the 10 woodworkers master one craft, cutting waste by 12% and sharpening the brand for boutique retailers [k]. scenario_stem:
QuickQuill Printing Ltd is a print shop in the commuter town of Redford, operating for 6 years. It produces business cards, menus and leaflets for local firms, employing 8 staff and 2 apprentices. Revenue was $520,000 last year, and orders have risen 15% since a rival closed. The shop now turns away work most Saturdays because both presses are fully booked.

Owner Nadia Rahman must choose how to expand. Buying a faster digital press costing $110,000 would raise capacity from 9,000 to 14,000 sheets per hour and last 10 years. Alternatively, hiring 3 more operators at $27,000 each per year would add 20% capacity immediately. Nadia has $130,000 in the business account and worries about machine breakdowns and staff absence. The extra Saturday work is worth about $60,000 a year.
